summary: Specifies using the KeyNote trust-management system as an authorization extension in the TLS handshake, following the guidance in RFC 5878. Hello extensions confirm both sides support it before authorization data is exchanged. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers connect securely, they can also swap permission slips. This describes how to use one kind of permission slip during the handshake.

questions: how does keynote work with tls
subtitle: How to send KeyNote credentials during a TLS handshake, either inline or by URL.

tldr.problem: TLS authenticates a peer, but a peer may also need to show credentials that authorize it to do certain things.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers two authorization data types, 64 and 65, for the TLS authorization extensions. One carries a list of KeyNote assertions directly and the other carries a URL and hash from which the list is fetched.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational, Independent Submission document, and it has been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 6042 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 8996. It is an Independent Submission and not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard.

sections.title: KeyNote Credentials in TLS
sections.content:
This document defines the identifiers needed to exchange KeyNote credential assertions inside a TLS exchange, under the authorization extension guidelines of RFC 5878. Such assertions can authorize the client, the server or both to perform certain actions. In most uses they are signed with a public key, and the X.509 key and signature encoding makes it possible to add KeyNote-based authorization to the existing, unmodified X.509 authentication in TLS.

A list of credentials, for example a delegation chain, can be sent in one payload, or a URL pointing to the list can be sent instead. Normally at least one credential is issued to the public key the sender uses to authenticate in TLS, which appears in the Licensees field. That key is given to the KeyNote evaluation engine as the Action Authorizer.
sections.plainLanguage: A permission slip says who is allowed to do what. This RFC lets two computers swap permission slips while they are saying hello.

sections.title: The Assertion List Type
sections.content:
The first type is keynote_assertion_list(64) in the TLS Authorization Data Formats registry. Its data is a list of KeyNote credential assertions that follows the profile in RFC 2704. It travels inside an AuthorizationDataEntry as an opaque sequence of 1 to 2^16-1 bytes.

The list is ASCII-encoded and the signed assertions are separated by two newline characters. A KeyNote assertion is like a public key certificate, except that it binds public keys to authorization rules rather than binding a name to a key. The receiver should set ACTION_AUTHORIZER to the sender's public key used to authenticate the TLS exchange. If another authentication mechanism is used, the credential issuer is responsible for issuing the appropriate credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The permission slips are written out as plain text, one after another, with a blank line between them. The receiver checks they belong to the person who is connecting.

sections.title: The Assertion List URL Type
sections.content:
The second type is keynote_assertion_list_url(65). It carries a URLandHash structure instead of the list. The receiver fetches the same kind of assertion list from the URL, and a one-way hash is included so it can check it got the intended one.

Implementations that support this type MUST support HTTP URLs. They MUST confirm that the hash of the fetched data matches the hash received in the handshake. A mismatch SHOULD be treated as though no authorization was provided, which leads to a bad_certificate alert. Other schemes may be supported, but circular dependencies MUST be avoided when fetching. Avoiding TLS for the fetch is one way to do that, so a client using HTTP MUST NOT use these TLS extensions if the HTTP Upgrade mechanism is in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of carrying all the slips, you can carry a note saying where to find them, plus a fingerprint so nobody can swap in different slips.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered two new entries in the TLS Authorization Data Formats registry, which is defined in RFC 5878: keynote_assertion_list(64) and keynote_assertion_list_url(65). Appendix A repeats the relevant data structures from RFC 5878 with these two entries added, including the hash lengths for the URL form.
sections.plainLanguage: The two new kinds of permission slip got official numbers, 64 and 65, in a public list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that there are no security considerations beyond those discussed in RFC 2704 (KeyNote), RFC 2792 (key and signature encoding) and RFC 5878 (TLS authorization extensions). The text itself adds nothing further.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say the safety rules are already written in three other documents, so they just point to those.
